plan: [With five bidders and a third-price rule, the winner pays the third-highest opponent bid. Without history and given independent private values, overbidding risks winning when the third-price exceeds my value. A conservative, robust approach is to bid my true value ($23), which avoids deliberate overbidding losses while still winning when the third-price is below my value. This is a safe baseline given no prior rounds to learn opponent behavior.]

[Assume other bidders bid their true values. If I bid b and win, that means all four others ≤ b; then expected third-highest equals the second-highest among four draws = (3/5)b. Win probability = (b/49)^4. Expected profit = (b/49)^4*(18 - 0.6b). Maximize w.r.t b → b = (4/3)*18 = 24. So overbidding to $24 maximizes expected payoff under this model.]

[I treat other bidders' values as iid uniform; if they bid their values then bidding b wins with prob (b/49)^4 and the payment conditional on winning ≈ expected 2nd-highest among 4 equals (3/5)b. Expected payoff ∝ (b/49)^4*(39 - 0.6b), which is increasing for b≤49 (optimum at b=52>49). So bid the maximum 49 to maximize expected profit.]

[Given a third-price sealed-bid with 5 bidders and independent uniform values, a symmetric equilibrium bids the expected third-highest conditional on winning. If my value is v, the four opponents are iid on [0,v], and their second-highest (the auction payment) has expectation 3/5·v. To maximize long-run profit I therefore bid 0.6×38 = 22.8, balancing win probability against expected payment.]

[This is a 3rd-price auction with n=5 and uniform independent values. The symmetric Bayes–Nash equilibrium bidding function for k=3 is b(v) = ((n-1)/(n-k+1))·v = (4/3)·v. With my value v = 16, the equilibrium bid is 64/3 ≈ 21.33. Rounding to the required $0.1 increment gives a bid of $21.3, which maximizes expected profit in the long run under symmetric play.]
